==Kroger Marketplace==
[[File:The exterior of a Kroger Marketplace store in Athens, Georgia 04.jpg|thumb|Exterior of a Kroger Marketplace in [[Athens, Georgia]]]]
'''Kroger Marketplace''' is a chain of [[hypermarket]]s. The brand was introduced in 2004 in the [[Columbus, Ohio]], area, which lost the [[Big Bear Stores|Big Bear]] and Big Bear Plus chains in [[Penn Traffic]]'s [[Chapter 11, Title 11, United States Code|Chapter 11 bankruptcy]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bizjournals.com/columbus/stories/2004/11/08/story8.html|title=Kroger hopes Graceland store is Wal-Mart antidote|last=Showalter|first=Kathy|date=November 8, 2004|website=www.bizjournals.com|access-date=July 31, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170731233015/https://www.bizjournals.com/columbus/stories/2004/11/08/story8.html|archive-date=July 31, 2017|url-status=live}}</ref> The Kroger Marketplace format is based on the [[Fry's Food and Drug#Fry's Marketplace|Fry's Marketplace]] stores that the Arizona division of Kroger is currently operating. There are currently a total of 188 marketplaces.<ref name=ourbusiness/>

Similar to rival chains [[Meijer]], [[Kmart (United States)|Kmart]], [[Target Corporation|Target]], [[Walmart]], and Albertsons, the stores are modeled after Kroger-owned Fred Meyer which house multiple departments.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/10/06/business/an-identity-crisis-for-supermarkets.html|title=An Identity Crisis for Supermarkets|last=Warner|first=Melanie|date=October 6, 2005|newspaper=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|access-date=January 24, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170715212524/http://www.nytimes.com/2005/10/06/business/an-identity-crisis-for-supermarkets.html|archive-date=July 15, 2017|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.enquirer.com/editions/2004/08/01/biz_groceryfight25.html|title=Kroger KEEPS LEAD|website=www.enquirer.com|access-date=January 24, 2017}}{{Dead link|date=July 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> In addition to the grocery department, stores typically include a [[Fred Meyer Jewelers]], [[Starbucks]], [[Donatos Pizza]], an in-store bank, and sections for toys, appliances, home furnishings as well as bed and bath—a format Big Bear had in their stores in the Columbus area.

In 2005, the company began renovating many Kroger Food & Drug stores in Ohio to an expanded and updated look, converting them to the Kroger Marketplace format.

==Manufacturing and distribution==
[[File:The_interior_produce_section_of_a_Kroger_Marketplace_store_in_Athens,_Georgia_03.jpg|thumb|Interior of a typical Kroger produce section]]
Food distribution and buying takes place under various subsidiaries and divisions. These include:<ref>{{cite web|title=Standard Vendor Agreement for Merchandise (Products)|date=January 2013|url=http://www.thekrogerco.com/docs/default-document-library/standard-vendor-agreement-(sva)-document-merchandising.pdf|publisher=Kroger|access-date=December 17, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131217235042/http://www.thekrogerco.com/docs/default-document-library/standard-vendor-agreement-(sva)-document-merchandising.pdf|archive-date=December 17, 2013|url-status=dead|df=dmy-all}}</ref>
* Kroger Group Cooperative, Inc.
* Kroger Group, Inc.
* Peytons
* WESCO
* Inter-American Products

Kroger operates its own fleet of trucks and trailers to distribute products to its various stores, in addition to contracts with various trucking companies.<ref name= proxystatement>{{cite web|url=https://www.wsj.com/market-data/quotes/KR/financials/annual/income-statement|title=2022 Kroger Financial Statements|publisher=The Kroger Co|access-date=June 11, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161226060558/https://www.google.com/finance?q=NYSE%3AKR&fstype=ii&ei=azu7Vsn8ItfKuATZ9Z_QCg|archive-date=December 26, 2016|url-status=live}}</ref> In June 2018, Kroger announced testing [[Autonomous car|driverless cars]] for delivering groceries. For this, Kroger is partnering with autonomous car company [[Nuro]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2018/06/27/kroger-to-soon-begin-driverless-grocery-delivery.html|title=An unmanned car may soon deliver your Kroger groceries|last=Hirsch|first=Lauren|date=June 28, 2018|work=CNBC|access-date=June 29, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180628211711/https://www.cnbc.com/2018/06/27/kroger-to-soon-begin-driverless-grocery-delivery.html|archive-date=June 28, 2018|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/2018/06/28/kroger-test-grocery-delivery-using-driverless-vehicles/741371002/|title=Kroger to test grocery delivery using driverless vehicles|work=USA TODAY|access-date=June 29, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180629005725/https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/2018/06/28/kroger-test-grocery-delivery-using-driverless-vehicles/741371002/|archive-date=June 29, 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>

In addition to stocking a variety of regional brand products, The Kroger Company also employs one of the largest networks of private label manufacturing in the country. Thirty-three plants (either wholly owned or used with operating agreements) in seventeen states create about 40% of Kroger's private label products.<ref name= proxystatement/> Similar to most major supermarket retailers, Kroger uses a three-tiered [[private label]] marketing strategy. One private brand emphasizes no-frills products at the lowest possible price, another is intended to be comparable to leading national brands but a better value and the third is a premium (often organic) brand.

==Private label brands==
Kroger offers a collection of its own branded products, referred to by the retailer as "Our Brands". The products are produced and sold in quality tiers, and account for over 30% of the retailer's unit sales.<ref>{{cite web|title=Three-Tier Marketing Strategy|url=http://www.thekrogerco.com/about-kroger/operations/manufacturing|publisher=Kroger|access-date=December 17, 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131023125344/http://www.thekrogerco.com/about-kroger/operations/manufacturing|archive-date=October 23, 2013|df=mdy-all}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Sparkly unicorn ice cream: Kroger's bid to win grocery wars|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-kroger-brands/sparkly-unicorn-ice-cream-krogers-bid-to-win-grocery-wars-idUSKCN1TL1A1|work=Reuters|access-date=July 1, 2019|df=mdy-all|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190701234051/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-kroger-brands/sparkly-unicorn-ice-cream-krogers-bid-to-win-grocery-wars-idUSKCN1TL1A1|archive-date=July 1, 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Banner Brand===
Banner Brand items are goods that bear the name of Kroger or its subsidiaries (i.e., Ralphs, King Soopers, etc.) or make reference to them (i.e., Big K), and are offered exclusively within Kroger-owned stores. These products are marketed to customers as budget-friendly, and account for over $13 billion in annual sales.<ref>{{cite news|title=The Simple Truth: Private Selection, other Kroger brands drive sales|url=https://www.cincinnati.com/story/money/2017/07/27/kroger-gins-up-own-goods-win-thrifty-consumers/472740001/|newspaper=Cincinnati.com|access-date=July 1, 2019|df=mdy-all|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190828223320/https://www.cincinnati.com/story/money/2017/07/27/kroger-gins-up-own-goods-win-thrifty-consumers/472740001/|archive-date=August 28, 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> Many of Kroger's health and beauty goods, one of the company's fastest-growing private label categories, are manufactured by third-party providers; these products include goods like [[ibuprofen]] and contact lens solution.

Manufacturers include Midwest Poultry Services (eggs).<ref name="fda-eggs-26-kroger-mps">{{cite web |title=Outbreak Investigation of Salmonella: Eggs (July 2026) |url=https://www.fda.gov/food/outbreaks-foodborne-illness/outbreak-investigation-salmonella-eggs-july-2026 |publisher=Food and Drug Administration |access-date=15 August 2026}}</ref>

===Private Selection===

Products marked ''Private Selection'' are offered to compare with gourmet brands or regional brands that may be considered more upscale than the standard Kroger brand products.

===Simple Truth===
''Simple Truth'' is Kroger's flagship natural and organic brand, and has grown quickly since its launch in 2012. The brand's launch marked the first time Kroger had delved into making its own gluten-free products, including flour mixes, bread, etc. The Simple Truth brand became the first Kroger offering to be introduced in China, on [[Alibaba Group|Alibaba's]] [[Tmall]] platform.<ref>{{cite news|title=Kroger partners with Alibaba in China grocery sales venture|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-kroger-alibaba/kroger-partners-with-alibaba-in-china-grocery-sales-venture-idUSKBN1KZ256|work=Reuters|access-date=July 1, 2019|df=mdy-all|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190701234052/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-kroger-alibaba/kroger-partners-with-alibaba-in-china-grocery-sales-venture-idUSKBN1KZ256|archive-date=July 1, 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> Simple Truth reached $2 billion in annual sales in 2018.<ref>{{cite news|title=Kroger's Simple Truth Brand Reaches $2 Billion in Annual Sales|work=MarketWatch |url=https://www.marketwatch.com/press-release/krogers-simple-truth-brand-reaches-2-billion-in-annual-sales-2018-01-25|publisher=Market Watch|access-date=July 1, 2019|df=mdy-all|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190701234052/https://www.marketwatch.com/press-release/krogers-simple-truth-brand-reaches-2-billion-in-annual-sales-2018-01-25|archive-date=July 1, 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Smart Way ===
''Smart Way'' is Kroger's budget-priced private label line that includes around 150 products. This line, which launched in two waves starting in September 2022, consolidates 16 legacy brands at a "new opening price-point".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kroger Announces New Smart Way Product Line |url=https://ir.kroger.com/news/news-details/2022/Kroger-Announces-New-Smart-Way-Product-Line/default.aspx |access-date=2025-03-31 |website=ir.kroger.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

The brands listed below may be found in various Kroger-owned stores.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.kroger.com/b/ourbrands |title=Kroger - Our Brands |access-date=July 1, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191105002445/https://www.kroger.com/b/ourbrands |archive-date=November 5, 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Other operations==
===Pharmacy Group===
Kroger previously owned and operated the SupeRx drug store chain. In 1985, Kroger outbid [[Rite Aid]] for the [[Hook's Drug Stores]] chain, based in [[Indianapolis]], Indiana, and combined it with SupeRx to become Hook's-SupeRx. In 1994, Kroger decided to exit the stand-alone drugstore business and sold its Hook's and SupeRx stores to [[Revco]], which later was sold to [[CVS Caremark|CVS]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://hooksmuseum.org/our-history/ |title=Our History |location=Indianapolis, Indiana |publisher=Hook's Drug Store Museum and Soda Fountain |access-date=December 17, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131218052508/http://hooksmuseum.org/our-history/ |archive-date=December 18, 2013 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Today, Kroger operates 2,252 pharmacies, most of which are located inside its supermarkets.<ref name=ourbusiness/> The Kroger Pharmacies continue as a profitable portion of the business and have been expanding to now include pharmacies in City Market, Dillons, Fred Meyer, Fry's, King Soopers, QFC, Ralphs, Harris Teeter, Smith's Food and Drug, and Kroger Supermarkets.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://jobs.kroger.com/kroger/go/Pharmacy-Jobs/395412/|title=Pharmacy Careers|publisher=Kroger|access-date=December 17, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131217234442/http://jobs.kroger.com/kroger/go/Pharmacy-Jobs/395412/|archive-date=December 17, 2013|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Supermarket Petroleum Group===
Since 1998, Kroger has added fuel centers in the parking lots of its supermarkets. More recently, the company has begun opening standalone fuel centers, often near stores whose parking lots could not accommodate a fuel center. As of Q2 2022, Kroger operated 1,629 supermarket fuel centers.<ref name=ourbusiness/><ref name=opera/>

In 2006, Kroger introduced a new common [[logo]] for all of its convenience store chains that is now also used at the fuel centers of all of its supermarket chains—a [[rhombus]] with a white, [[stylized art|stylized image]] of the [[continental United States]] in the center bordered by four colored areas: dark blue representing the Pacific Ocean, red representing Canada, green representing the Atlantic Ocean, and yellow representing the [[Gulf of Mexico]]. This logo is also still used at the convenience stores that were sold to EG Group in 2018.

===Kroger Personal Finance===
Kroger Personal Finance was introduced in 2007 to offer branded [[Visa Inc.|Visa]] cards, mortgages, home equity loans, pet, renter's and home insurance, [[identity theft]] protection, and wireless services.<ref name= proxystatement/> In 2017, MasterCard became the network for Kroger's newly branded 1-2-3 REWARDS credit card issued by U.S. Bank.<ref>{{cite web |title=Mastercard Selected for Kroger Co-Brand Credit Card Issued by U.S. Bank |url=https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20170727005891/en/Mastercard-Selected-Kroger-Co-Brand-Credit-Card-Issued |website=Business Wire |date=July 27, 2017 |access-date=6 May 2020}}</ref> In 2019, Kroger banned the use of Visa credit cards (but not debit cards) at two of its subsidiary chains: Foods Co. Supermarkets and Smiths, citing rising costs from premium cards.<ref>{{cite web |title=Large grocery chain widens ban on Visa credit cards |url=https://www.americanbanker.com/articles/large-grocery-chain-widens-ban-on-visa-credit-cards |website=American Banker |date=March 2019 |publisher=Arizent |access-date=6 May 2020 |archive-date=August 9, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200809053745/https://www.americanbanker.com/articles/large-grocery-chain-widens-ban-on-visa-credit-cards |url-status=dead }}</ref>  In July 2026, it was announced the Kroger Mastercard would be discontinued and existing users would be transitioned automatically to a new card offered by [[U.S. Bancorp|U.S. Bank]].<ref>{{Cite web | title=Kroger's credit card is going away: Here is what you need to know | url=https://www.wcpo.com/money/consumer/dont-waste-your-money/krogers-credit-card-is-going-away-here-is-what-you-need-to-know-about-lost-perks-and-new-benefits | access-date=2026-08-15 | website=www.wcpo.com}}</ref>

=== 84.51° ===
84.51° is a wholly owned subsidiary of Kroger engaged in data science and consumer insights, created in April 2015, as a result of Kroger purchasing the remaining half of its then-joint venture [[Dunnhumby|Dunnhumby USA]] from [[Tesco]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/tomdavenport/2018/04/02/84-51-builds-a-machine-learning-machine-for-kroger/#1458ccb264e1|title=84.51° Builds a Machine Learning Machine for Kroger|last=Davenport|first=Tom|date=April 2, 2018|website=Forbes|access-date=September 26, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200804210544/https://www.forbes.com/sites/tomdavenport/2018/04/02/84-51-builds-a-machine-learning-machine-for-kroger/#1458ccb264e1|archive-date=August 4, 2020|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Pricing discrepancies and overcharges ==
In 2025, an investigation by ''[[The Guardian]]'', Consumer Reports, and the ''[[Food & Environment Reporting Network]]'' revealed widespread overcharging at Kroger stores across multiple states due to expired sale tags leading to higher prices at checkout.<ref name="Guardian20253">{{Cite web |title='Customers are being duped': how murky grocery sales tactics are squeezing some Kroger shoppers |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2025/may/14/kroger-supermarket-sales-tactics |access-date=2025-05-14 |website=The Guardian|date=May 14, 2025 |last1=Hudson |first1=Michael |last2=Genoways |first2=Ted |last3=Kravitz |first3=Derek |last4=Ross |first4=Theodore }}</ref> Tests in 26 stores across 14 states and Washington, D.C., identified over 150 items with expired sale tags, averaging a $1.70 overcharge per item, or 18% above the advertised sale price.<ref name="Guardian20253" /> In Colorado, union tests at over 30 King Soopers stores found more than 300 expired tags, with overcharges averaging nearly 15%.<ref name="Guardian20253" /> An internal Kroger audit at one western U.S. store reported approximately 6% of price tags were incorrect, exceeding the company’s 1% error threshold.<ref name="Guardian20253" /> The investigation, supported by customer complaints and union reports, linked the issue to chronic understaffing, with expired tags remaining on shelves for weeks.<ref name="Guardian20253" /> Kroger denied systemic pricing issues, asserting that errors were a small fraction of billions of annual transactions and emphasizing regular audits to ensure pricing accuracy.<ref name="Guardian20253" />

[[File:Google 2026 logo.svg|thumb|Google's logo]]

[[Google]] is a [[computer software]] and a [[web search engine]] company that acquired, on average, more than one company per week in 2010 and 2011.<ref>{{cite news|last=Rusli|first=Evelyn M.|title=For Google, a New High in Deal-Making|url=https://dealbook.nytimes.com/2011/10/27/google-hits-new-ma-record/|work=The New York Times|access-date=December 7, 2011|date=October 27, 2011}}</ref> The table below is an incomplete list of acquisitions, with each acquisition listed being for the respective company in its entirety, unless otherwise specified. The [[takeover|acquisition]] date listed is the date of the agreement between Google and the acquisition subject. As Google is headquartered in the United States, acquisition is listed in [[US dollars]]. If the price of an acquisition is unlisted, then it is undisclosed. If the Google service that is derived from the acquired company is known, then it is also listed here. Google itself was re-organized into a subsidiary of a larger holding company known as [[Alphabet Inc.]] in 2015.

[[File:Google timeline.svg|thumb|Timeline of Google products, services, and acquisitions ending in 2015]]
{{As of|2025|03}}, Alphabet has acquired over 200 companies, with its largest acquisition being the purchase of [[Wiz (company)|Wiz]], a cloud security company, for $32 billion in 2025 (the acquisition received unconditional approval from the European Union in February 2026<ref>{{Cite news |date=2026-02-10 |title=EU clears Google's $32 billion bid for Wiz cybersecurity company |url=https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/tech/technology/eu-clears-googles-32-bn-bid-for-wiz-cybersecurity-company/articleshow/128166636.cms |access-date=2026-02-10 |work=The Economic Times |issn=0013-0389}}</ref><ref>Chee, F. Y. (2026, February 10). [https://www.reuters.com/world/google-secures-eu-antitrust-approval-32-billion-wiz-acquisition-2026-02-10/ Google secures EU antitrust approval for $32 billion Wiz acquisition]. Reuters. </ref>). Most of the firms acquired by Google are based in the United States, and, in turn, most of these are based in or around the [[San Francisco Bay Area]]. To date, Alphabet has divested itself of four<ref>{{cite news|title=SketchUp Is Google's First Divestment In Years, And It Made A Profit|first=Josh|last=Constine|date=April 26, 2012|work=[[TechCrunch]]|url=https://techcrunch.com/2012/04/26/sketchup-google-first-divestment/|access-date=April 6, 2013}}</ref> business units: [[Frommers]], which was sold back to Arthur Frommer in April 2012;<ref>{{cite web|title=Frommer's founder buys back travel guide brand from Google|first=Julianne|last=Pepitone|date=April 4, 2013|publisher=[[CNNMoney.com]]|url=https://money.cnn.com/2013/04/04/technology/google-frommer/index.html?source=cnn_bin|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130407071833/http://money.cnn.com/2013/04/04/technology/google-frommer/index.html?source=cnn_bin|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 7, 2013|access-date=May 6, 2013}}</ref> [[SketchUp]], which was sold to [[Trimble Navigation|Trimble]] in April 2012,<ref>{{cite web|title=A new home for SketchUp|first=John|last=Bacus|publisher=[[SketchUp]]|date=April 26, 2012|url=http://sketchupdate.blogspot.com/2012/04/new-home-for-sketchup.html|access-date=May 6, 2013}}</ref> [[Boston Dynamics]] in early 2016 and Google Radio Automation, which was sold to WideOrbit in 2009.<ref>{{cite web|title=WideOrbit Acquires Google Radio Automation|date=August 5, 2009|publisher=WideOrbit|url=http://www.wideorbit.com/news-archives/3-news/news-archives/141-wideorbit-acquires-google-radio-automation/|access-date=May 6, 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130317121019/http://www.wideorbit.com/news-archives/3-news/news-archives/141-wideorbit-acquires-google-radio-automation/|archive-date=March 17, 2013}}</ref>

Many [[Google products]] originated as services provided by companies that Google has since acquired. For example, Google's first acquisition was the [[Usenet]] company Deja News, and its services became [[Google Groups]]. Similarly, Google acquired [[Dodgeball (service)|Dodgeball]], a [[social networking service]] company, and eventually replaced it with [[Google Latitude]]. Other acquisitions include [[web application]] company JotSpot, which became [[Google Sites]]; [[Voice over IP]] company GrandCentral, which became [[Google Voice]]; and [[video hosting service]] company Next New Networks, which became [[YouTube Next Lab and Audience Development Group]]. CEO Larry Page has explained that potential acquisition candidates must pass a sort of "toothbrush test": Are their products potentially useful once or twice a day, and do they improve your life?<ref>{{cite web|title=In Silicon Valley, Mergers Must Meet the Toothbrush Test|date=August 17, 2014|website=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://dealbook.nytimes.com/2014/08/17/in-silicon-valley-mergers-must-meet-the-toothbrush-test/?_php=true&_type=blogs&_php=true&_type=blogs&_r=1&/|access-date=August 18, 2014}}</ref>

Following the acquisition of Israel-based startup [[Waze]] in June 2013, Google submitted a [[10-Q]] filing with the Securities Exchange Commission (SEC) that revealed that the corporation spent $1.3 billion on acquisitions during the first half of 2013, with $966 million of that total going to Waze.<ref name="Rip">{{cite web|title=Yahoo And Google Are Both Spending Big Money On Acquisition Sprees And What That Says About Their Futures|url=https://techcrunch.com/2013/07/29/yahoo-and-google-are-both-spending-big-money-on-acquisition-sprees-and-what-that-says-about-their-futures/?ncid=tcdaily|work=TechCrunch|publisher=AOL Inc|access-date=July 29, 2013|first=Rip|last=Empson|date=July 29, 2013}}</ref>

== Key Acquisitions==
In October 2006, Google announced that it had acquired the video-sharing site [[YouTube]] for $1.65&nbsp;billion in Google stock,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://techcrunch.com/2006/10/09/google-has-acquired-youtube/|title=Google Has Acquired YouTube|last=Arrington|first=Michael|date=October 9, 2006|website=[[TechCrunch]]|publisher=[[AOL]]|access-date=March 15, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/10/09/business/09cnd-deal.html|title=Google to Acquire YouTube for $1.65 Billion|last1=Sorkin|first1=Andrew Ross|last2=Peters|first2=Jeremy W.|date=October 9, 2006|website=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=March 15, 2017}}</ref> and the deal was finalized on November 13, 2006.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://techcrunch.com/2006/11/13/google-closes-youtube-acquisition/|title=Google Closes YouTube Acquisition|last=Arrington|first=Michael|date=November 13, 2006|website=[[TechCrunch]]|publisher=[[AOL]]|access-date=March 15, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-google-idUSWEN973120061114|title=Google closes YouTube deal|last=Auchard|first=Eric|date=November 14, 2006|website=[[Reuters]]|publisher=[[Thomson Reuters]]|access-date=March 15, 2017}}</ref>

On April 13, 2007, Google reached an agreement to acquire [[DoubleClick]] for $3.1&nbsp;billion, transferring to Google valuable relationships that DoubleClick had with Web publishers and advertising agencies.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/04/14/technology/14DoubleClick.html|title=Google Buys DoubleClick for $3.1 Billion|last1=Story|first1=Louise|last2=Helft|first2=Miguel|date=April 14, 2007|website=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=March 9, 2017}}</ref> The deal was approved despite anti-trust concerns raised by competitors [[Microsoft]] and [[AT&T]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Googled: The End of the World As We Know It|last=Auletta|first=Ken|date=2009|publisher=The Penguin Press|isbn=9780753522431|location=New York|language=en}}</ref>

On August 15, 2011, Google made what was, at its time, its largest-ever acquisition to date when it announced that it would acquire [[Motorola Mobility]] for $12.5&nbsp;billion<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/faster-forward/post/google-agrees-to-acquire-motorola-mobility/2011/08/15/gIQABmTkGJ_blog.html|title=Google agrees to acquire Motorola Mobility|author=Tsukayama, Hayley|date=August 15, 2011|newspaper=The Washington Post|access-date=August 17, 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://investor.google.com/releases/2011/0815.html|title=Google to Acquire Motorola Mobility&nbsp;— Google Investor Relations|website=Google|access-date=August 17, 2011}}</ref> subject to approval from regulators in the United States and Europe. This purchase was made in part to help Google gain Motorola's considerable patent portfolio on mobile phones and wireless technologies, to help protect Google in its ongoing patent disputes with other companies,<ref name="supercharging android">{{cite web|url=http://googleblog.blogspot.com/2011/08/supercharging-android-google-to-acquire.html|title=Official Google Blog: Supercharging Android: Google to Acquire Motorola Mobility|last=Page|first=Larry|website=Google Blog at Blogspot.com|access-date=August 17, 2011}}</ref> mainly [[Apple Inc.|Apple]] and [[Microsoft]],<ref name="appleinsider1">{{cite web|url=https://www.appleinsider.com/articles/11/08/15/google_ceo_anticompetitive_apple_microsoft_forced_motorola_deal.html|title=Google CEO: 'Anticompetitive' Apple, Microsoft forced Motorola deal|last=Hughes|first=Neil|website=AppleInsider|date=August 15, 2011 |access-date=August 17, 2011}}</ref> and to allow it to continue to freely offer [[Android (operating system)|Android]].<ref name="cnet">{{cite web|url=http://news.cnet.com/8301-1035_3-20092362-94/google-to-buy-motorola-mobility-for-$12.5b/|title=Google to buy Motorola Mobility for $12.5B|last=Cheng|first=Roger|date=August 15, 2011|website=CNet News}}</ref> The merger was completed on May 22, 2012, after the approval of China.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-18164190|title=Google|date=May 22, 2012|work=BBC News|access-date=May 23, 2012}}</ref>

In June 2013, Google acquired [[Waze]], a $966 million deal.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cnet.com/news/google-reveals-it-spent-966-million-in-waze-acquisition/|title=Google reveals it spent $966 million in Waze acquisition|last=Kerr|first=Dara|date=July 25, 2013|website=[[CNET]]|publisher=[[CBS Interactive]]|access-date=June 12, 2017}}</ref> While Waze would remain an independent entity, its social features, such as its crowdsourced location platform, were reportedly valuable integrations between Waze and [[Google Maps]], Google's own mapping service.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://techcrunch.com/2013/06/11/its-official-google-buys-waze-giving-a-social-data-boost-to-its-location-and-mapping-business/|title=Google Bought Waze For $1.1B, Giving A Social Data Boost To Its Mapping Business|last=Lunden|first=Ingrid|date=June 11, 2013|website=[[TechCrunch]]|publisher=[[AOL]]|access-date=June 12, 2017}}</ref>

On January 26, 2014, Google announced it had agreed to acquire [[DeepMind Technologies]], a privately held artificial intelligence company from [[London]]. DeepMind describes itself as having the ability to combine the best techniques from machine learning and systems neuroscience to build general-purpose learning algorithms. DeepMind's first commercial applications were used in simulations, e-commerce and games. {{As of|2013|12|post=,}} it was reported that DeepMind had roughly 75 employees.<ref name="Chowdhry-DeepMind">{{cite news|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/amitchowdhry/2014/01/27/google-to-acquire-artificial-intelligence-company-deepmind/|title=Google To Acquire Artificial Intelligence Company DeepMind|last=Chowdhry|first=Amit|date=January 27, 2014|newspaper=Forbes|access-date=January 27, 2014}}</ref> Technology news website ''[[Recode]]'' reported that the company was purchased for $400 million though it was not disclosed where the information came from. A Google spokesman would not comment on the price.<ref name="Helgren- DeepMind">{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-google-deepmind-idUSBREA0Q03220140127|title=Google to buy artificial intelligence company DeepMind|last=Helgren|first=Chris|date=January 27, 2014|newspaper=Reuters|access-date=January 27, 2014|archive-date=September 26, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150926065732/http://www.reuters.com/article/2014/01/27/us-google-deepmind-idUSBREA0Q03220140127|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Ribeiro- DeepMind">{{cite news|url=http://www.pcworld.com/article/2091500/google-acquires-artificial-intelligence-company-deepmind.html|title=Google buys artificial intelligence company DeepMind|last=Ribeiro|first=Jon|date=January 27, 2014|newspaper=PC World|access-date=January 27, 2014}}</ref> The purchase of DeepMind aids in Google's recent growth in the artificial intelligence and robotics community.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theverge.com/2014/1/26/5348640/google-deepmind-acquisition-robotics-ai|title=Google buying AI startup DeepMind for a reported $400 million|last=Opam|first=Kwame|date=January 26, 2014|website=[[The Verge]]|publisher=[[Vox Media]]|access-date=March 9, 2017}}</ref>

== Divestitures ==
On December 10, 2012, Google sold the manufacturing operations of Motorola Mobility to [[Flextronics]] for $75&nbsp;million.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.engadget.com/2012/12/11/motorola-flextronics/|title=Motorola's retreat continues, sells factories in China and Brazil to Flextronics for $75 million|last=Cooper|first=Daniel|date=December 11, 2012|website=[[Engadget]]|publisher=[[AOL]]|access-date=March 9, 2017}}</ref> As a part of the agreement, Flextronics will manufacture undisclosed Android and other mobile devices.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.zdnet.com/article/flextronics-acquires-motorola-mobilitys-plants-in-china-brazil/|title=Flextronics acquires Motorola Mobility's plants in China, Brazil|date=December 11, 2012|work=ZDNet}}</ref> On December 19, 2012, Google sold the Motorola Home business division of Motorola Mobility to [[Arris Group]] for $2.35&nbsp;billion in a cash-and-stock transaction. As a part of this deal, Google acquired a 15.7% stake in Arris Group valued at $300&nbsp;million.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theverge.com/2012/12/19/3786086/google-sells-motorola-home-to-arris-for-2-35-billion-in-cash-and-stock|title=Google sells Motorola Home set top box division to Arris for $2.35 billion|last=Seifert|first=Dan|date=December 19, 2012|website=[[The Verge]]|publisher=[[Vox Media]]|access-date=April 7, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://techcrunch.com/2012/12/19/motorola-home-finds-a-new-home-at-arris-google-sells-broadband-unit-for-2-35b-to-double-down-on-mobile/|title=Motorola Home Finds A New Home At Arris. Google Sells Broadband Unit For $2.35B To Double Down On Mobile|last=Lardinois|first=Frederic|date=December 19, 2012|website=[[TechCrunch]]|publisher=[[AOL]]|access-date=April 7, 2017}}</ref>

On January 29, 2014, Google announced that it would divest Motorola Mobility to [[Lenovo]] for $2.91 billion, a fraction of the original $12.5 billion price paid by Google to acquire the company. Google retained all but 2000 of Motorola's patents and entered into cross-licensing deals.<ref name="Opan- DeepMind- Post">{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/technology/google-sells-motorola-mobility-to-lenovo-for-291-billion/2014/01/29/92836bce-8932-11e3-833c-33098f9e5267_story.html|title=Google sells Motorola Mobility to Lenovo for $2.91 billion|last=Kang|first=Cecilia|date=January 30, 2014|newspaper=The Washington Post|access-date=January 30, 2014}}</ref>

In 2017, Google sold off its satellite business, Terra Bella, to [[Planet Labs]] for an undisclosed price and entered into a multi-year agreement to license Earth imagery from the company.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://techcrunch.com/2017/02/03/google-selling-terra-bella-satellite-imaging-business-to-planet/|title=Google selling Terra Bella satellite imaging business to Planet|last=Etherington|first=Darrell|date=February 3, 2017|website=TechCrunch|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170222062422/https://techcrunch.com/2017/02/03/google-selling-terra-bella-satellite-imaging-business-to-planet/|archive-date=February 22, 2017|access-date=December 18, 2019}}</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Mobile commerce
======================================================================

{{Short description|Commerce via hand held devices}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=August 2026}}
{{Ecommerce}}
The term '''mobile commerce''' was originally coined in 1997 by Kevin Duffey at the launch of the Global Mobile Commerce Forum, to mean "the delivery of [[electronic commerce]] capabilities directly into the consumer’s hand, anywhere, via [[Wireless communication|Wireless]] technology."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://cryptome.org/jya/glomob.htm|title=Global Mobile Commerce Forum}}</ref> Some choose to think of mobile commerce as meaning "a retail outlet in your customer’s pocket."

== History ==
The Global Mobile Commerce Forum, which came to include over 100 organisations, had its fully minuted launch in London on 10 November 1997. Kevin Duffey was elected Executive Chairman at the first meeting in November 1997.  The meeting was opened by Dr Mike Short, former chairman of the [[GSM]] Association, with the very first forecasts for mobile commerce from Kevin Duffey (Group Telecoms Director of [[Logica]]) and Tom Alexander (later CEO of [[Virgin Mobile]] and then of Orange). Over 100 companies joined the Forum within a year, a number of them forming mobile commerce teams of their own, e.g. [[Mastercard|MasterCard]] and Motorola. Among these one hundred companies, the first two were Logica and [[Cellnet]] (which later became O2). Member organisations such as [[Nokia]], Apple, [[Alcatel (mobile device brand)|Alcatel]], and [[Vodafone]] began a series of trials and collaborations.

Mobile commerce services were first delivered in 1997, when the first two mobile-phone-enabled [[Coca-Cola]] vending machines were installed in the [[Helsinki]] area in Finland. The machines accepted payment via [[SMS]] text messages. This work evolved into several new mobile applications, such as the first mobile phone-based banking service launched in 1997 by [[Merita Bank|Merita Bank of Finland]], also using SMS. [[Finnair]] mobile check-in was also a major milestone, first introduced in 2001.

The m-Commerce server developed in late 1997 by Kevin Duffey and Andrew Tobin at Logica won the 1998 [[Financial Times]] award for "most innovative mobile product," in a solution implemented with De La Rue, Motorola and Logica.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.prnewswire.co.uk/news-releases/de-la-rue-motorola-and-logica-win-financial-times-award-for-most-innovative-mobile-product-156092345.html|title=DE LA RUE, MOTOROLA AND LOGICA WIN FINANCIAL TIMES AWARD FOR MOST INNOVATIVE MOBILE PRODUCT /PR Newswire UK/|last=Logica}}</ref> The Financial Times commended the solution for "turning mobile commerce into a reality."{{citation needed|date=July 2015}}  The trademark for m-Commerce was filed on 7 April 2008.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.trademarkia.co.uk/uk/mcommerce-56494.htm|title=M-COMMERCE - Reviews & Brand Information - Logica Plc 250 Brook Drive Green Park, Reading GB RG2 6UA in European Community (CTM)|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150823025335/http://www.trademarkia.co.uk/uk/mcommerce-56494.htm|archive-date=23 August 2015}}</ref>

In 1998, the first sales of digital content as downloads to mobile phones were made possible when the first commercial downloadable [[ringtone]]s were launched in Finland by [[Radiolinja]] (now part of [[Elisa Oyj]]).

Two major national commercial platforms for mobile commerce were launched in 1999: Smart Money in the Philippines and [[NTT DoCoMo]]'s [[I-Mode]] Internet service in Japan. I-Mode offered a revenue-sharing plan where NTT DoCoMo kept 9 per cent of the fee users paid for content, and returned 91 percent to the content owner.

Mobile-commerce-related services spread rapidly in the early 2000s. Norway launched mobile parking payments. Austria offered train ticketing via mobile devices. Japan offered mobile purchases of airline tickets.

In April 2002, building on the work of the Global Mobile Commerce Forum (GMCF), the [[European Telecommunications Standards Institute]] (ETSI) appointed Joachim Hoffmann of Motorola to develop official standards for mobile commerce.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://portal.etsi.org/m-comm/summary.asp |title=Archived copy |access-date=2011-09-29 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150403000010/http://portal.etsi.org/m-comm/summary.asp |archive-date=3 April 2015 }}</ref> In appointing Mr Hoffman, ETSI quoted industry analysts as predicting "that m-commerce is poised for such an exponential growth over the next few years that could reach US$200 billion by 2004".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://portal.etsi.org/m-comm/m-comm_ToR.asp |title=Archived copy |access-date=2011-09-29 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140303231310/http://portal.etsi.org/m-comm/m-comm_ToR.asp |archive-date=3 March 2014 }}</ref>

As of 2008, UCL Computer Science and [[Peter J. Bentley]] demonstrated the potential for medical applications on mobile devices.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://apps.peterjbentley.com/Blog/?e=53483&d=08/29/2010&s=iStethoscope%20Pro%20in%20a%20medical%20journal|title=iStethoscope in Medical Journal|access-date=23 November 2010}}</ref>

In order to exploit the potential mobile commerce market, mobile phone manufacturers such as Nokia, Ericsson, Motorola, and [[Qualcomm]] are working with carriers such as AT&T Wireless and Sprint to develop [[Wireless Application Protocol|WAP]]-enabled smartphones. Smartphones offer fax, e-mail, and phone capabilities.

"[[Profitability]] for device vendors and carriers hinges on high-end mobile devices and the accompanying killer applications," said Burchett.{{Who|date=August 2010}} Perennial early adopters, such as the youth market, which are the least price sensitive, as well as more open to premium mobile content and applications, must also be a key target for device vendors.

Since the launch of the [[iPhone]] in 2007, mobile commerce has moved away from SMS systems and into actual applications.  SMS has significant [[security vulnerabilities]] and congestion problems, even though it is widely available and accessible. In addition, improvements in the capabilities of modern mobile devices make it prudent to place more of the resource burden on the mobile device.

Unlike online banking using bank websites, mobile banking allows a smaller number of operations based on short messages or applications installed on mobile devices. At present, it is estimated that by 2022, the number of customers adopting mobile banking will increase to 2 billion, and banks are investing more and more in improving mobile applications to improve security and customer satisfaction.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bucharest University of Economic Studies|last2=Hadad|first2=Shahrazad|date=2013|title=Challenges for Banking Services in the Knowledge Economy|url=http://www.managementdynamics.ro/index.php/journal/article/view/326/272|journal=Management Dynamics in the Knowledge Economy|volume=7|issue=3|pages=337–352|doi=10.25019/MDKE/7.3.04|s2cid=204842231|doi-access=free}}</ref>

More recently, [[brick and mortar business]] owners, and [[big-box store|big-box retailers]] in particular, have made an effort to take advantage of mobile commerce by utilizing a number of mobile capabilities such as [[location-based service]]s, [[Barcode reader#Cell phone cameras|barcode scanning]], and [[Apple Push Notification Service|push notifications]] to improve the customer experience of shopping in physical stores. By creating what is referred to as a 'bricks & clicks' environment, physical retailers can allow customers to access the common benefits of shopping online (such as product reviews, information, and coupons) while still shopping in the physical store. This is seen as a bridge between the gap created by e-commerce and in-store shopping, and is being utilized by physical retailers as a way to compete with the lower prices typically seen through online retailers. By midsummer 2013, "omnichannel" retailers (those with significant e-commerce and in-store sales) were seeing between 25% and 30% of traffic to their online properties originating from mobile devices. Some other pure play/online-only retail sites (especially those in the travel category) as well as flash sales sites and deal sites were seeing between 40% and 50% of traffic (and sometimes significantly more) originate from mobile devices.

Platforms such as [[Wix.com|Wix]], Dorik, and Duda are cloud-based website builders that enable businesses to create mobile-optimized storefronts without coding expertise.<ref>{{cite web |title=Best Ecommerce Website Builders 2026: Create an Online Store |website=Tech.co |date=2026-01-29 |url=https://tech.co/website-builders/best-ecommerce-website-builders |access-date=2026-02-27}}</ref> These services provide no‑code, template‑driven e-commerce site builders with AI tools.<ref>{{cite web |last=Masoner |first=Liz |title=10 Best Website Builders Of 2025 |website=Forbes Advisor |date=2024-12-19 |url=https://www.forbes.com/advisor/business/software/best-website-builders/ |access-date=2026-02-27}}</ref>

The [[Google Wallet]] Mobile App<ref>{{cite web|url=http://mashable.com/follow/topics/google-wallet/|title=Google Wallet|website=[[Mashable]]}}</ref> launched in September 2011 and the m-Commerce joint venture formed in June 2011 between Vodafone, O2, Orange and T-Mobile are recent developments of note.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mobileindustryawards.com/|title=Mobile Industry Awards|website=mobileindustryawards.com}}</ref> Reflecting the importance of m-Commerce, in April 2012 the Competition Commissioner of the European Commission ordered an in-depth investigation of the m-Commerce joint venture between Vodafone, O2, Orange and T-Mobile.<ref>{{cite web |date=16 April 2012 |title=Vodafone, EE and O2 still confident on m-commerce JV |url=http://www.mobilenewscwp.co.uk/2012/04/16/vodafone-everything-everywhere-and-o2-still-confident-on-m-commerce-jv/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130727111149/https://www.mobilenewscwp.co.uk/2012/04/16/vodafone-everything-everywhere-and-o2-still-confident-on-m-commerce-jv/ |archive-date=2013-07-27 |website=Mobile News}}</ref> A recent survey states that 2012, 41% of smartphone customers have purchased retail products with their mobile devices.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mercuryminds.com/blog/company_news/introducing-mobile-commerce-solutions-for-online-retailers|title=Introducing Mobile Commerce solutions for online-retailers|access-date=5 April 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130330115537/http://www.mercuryminds.com/blog/company_news/introducing-mobile-commerce-solutions-for-online-retailers|archive-date=30 March 2013}}</ref>

== Products and services available ==

===Mobile money transfer===
In Kenya money transfer is mainly done through the use of mobile phones. This was an initiative of a multimillion-shillings company in Kenya named Safaricom. Currently, the companies involved are Safaricom and Airtel. Mobile [[money transmitter|money transfer services]] in Kenya are now provided by the two companies under the names M-PESA and Airtel Money respectively.

A similar system called [[MobilePay]] has been operated by [[Danske Bank]] in Denmark since 2013. It gained considerable popularity with about 1.6 million users by mid-2015. Another similar system called [[Vipps]] was introduced in Norway in 2015.

A mobile automated teller machine (ATM) is a special type of ATM. Most ATMs are usually stationary, and they're often found attached to the side of financial institutions, in stores, and in malls. A mobile ATM, on the other hand, is meant to be moved from location to location. This type of ATM is often found at special events for which ATM service is only needed temporarily. For example, they may be found at carnivals, fairs, and parades. They may also be used at seminars and workshops where no regular ATM is nearby.

Mobile ATMs are usually self-contained units that don't need a building or enclosure. Usually, a mobile ATM can be placed in just about any location and can transmit transaction information wirelessly, so there's no need to have a phone line handy. Mobile ATMs may, however, require access to an electrical source, though there are some capable of running on alternative sources of power. Often, these units are constructed of weather-resistant materials, so they can be used in practically any type of weather. Additionally, these machines typically have internal heating and air conditioning units that help keep them functional despite the temperature of the environment.ion of mobile money services for the unbanked, operators are now looking for efficient ways to roll out and manage distribution networks that can support cash-in and cash-out. Unlike traditional ATMs, sicap Mobile ATMs have been specially engineered to connect to mobile money platforms and provide bank-grade ATM quality.
In Hungary, Vodafone allows cash or bank card payments for monthly phone bills.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.vodafone.hu/eng/support/questions-answers/pay-monthly/paying-your-bill|title = Hiba 404 &#124; Vodafone}}</ref> The Hungarian market is one where direct debits are not standard practice, so the facility eases the burden of queuing for the postpaid half of Vodafone's subscriber base in Hungary.

=== Mobile ticketing ===
{{Main|Mobile ticketing}}

Tickets can be sent to mobile phones using a variety of technologies.  Users are then able to use their tickets immediately, by presenting their mobile phone at the ticket check as a digital boarding pass. Most numbers of users are now moving towards this technology. The best example would be [[IRCTC]] where the ticket comes as an SMS to users. New technology such as [[Radio-frequency identification|RFID]] can now be used to directly provide a single association digital ticket via the mobile device hardware associated with relevant software.

=== Mobile vouchers, coupons and loyalty cards ===
Mobile ticketing technology can also be used for the distribution of vouchers, coupons, and loyalty cards.  These items are represented by a virtual token that is sent to the mobile phone. A customer presenting a mobile phone with one of these tokens at the [[point of sale]] receives the same benefits as if they had the traditional token.  Stores may send coupons to customers using [[location-based service]]s to determine when the customer is nearby. Using a connected device and the networking effect can also allow for gamification within the shopping experience.

=== Content purchase and delivery ===
Currently, mobile content purchase and delivery mainly consist of the sale of ring-tones, wallpapers, apps, and games for mobile phones.  The convergence of mobile phones, portable audio players, and video players into a single device is increasing the purchase and delivery of full-length music tracks and videos. The download speeds available with [[4G]] networks make it possible to buy a movie on a mobile device in a couple of seconds.{{citation needed|date=February 2023}}

=== Location-based services ===
{{Main|Location-based service}}
The location of the mobile phone user is an important piece of information used during mobile commerce or m-commerce transactions.  Knowing the location of the user allows for [[location-based service]]s such as:
* Local discount offers
* Local weather
* Tracking and monitoring of people
* Data-driven mashups targeting at a hyper-local level

=== Information services ===
A wide variety of information services can be delivered to mobile phone users in much the same way as it is delivered to PCs.  These services include:
* [[News]]
* [[Sales quote]]s
* Sports scores
* Financial records
* [[Traffic reporting]]
* Emergency Alerts
* [[Location Based Notifications]]

Customized traffic information, based on a user's actual travel patterns, can be sent to a mobile device. This customized data is more useful than a generic traffic-report broadcast but was impractical before the invention of modern mobile devices due to the [[Bandwidth (computing)|bandwidth]] requirements.

=== Mobile banking ===
{{Main|Mobile banking}}

Banks and other financial institutions use mobile commerce to allow their customers to access account information and make transactions, such as purchasing stocks, and remitting money.  This service is often referred to as ''[[mobile banking]]'', or m-banking.

=== Mobile brokerage ===
Stock market services offered via mobile devices have also become more popular and are known as Mobile Brokerage.  They allow the subscriber to react to market developments in a timely fashion and irrespective of their physical location.

=== Auctions ===

Over the past three years{{When|date=August 2010}} [[mobile reverse auction]] solutions have grown in popularity.{{By whom|date=August 2010}} Unlike traditional auctions, the reverse auction (or low-bid auction) bills the consumer's phone each time they place a bid. Multiple mobiles [[SMS]] commerce solutions rely on a one-time purchase or one-time subscription; however, reverse auctions offer a high return for the mobile vendor as they require the consumer to make multiple transactions over a long period of time.

=== Mobile browsing  ===
{{Main|Mobile browser}}
Using a mobile browser—a [[World Wide Web]] browser on a mobile device—customers can shop online without having to be at their personal computer. Multiple [[mobile marketing]] apps with geo-location capability are now delivering user-specific marketing messages to the right person at the right time.

=== Mobile purchase ===
[[Catalog merchants]] can accept orders from customers electronically, via the customer's mobile device.  In some cases, the merchant may even deliver the catalog electronically, rather than mailing a paper catalog to the customer. Consumers making mobile purchases can also receive value-add [[upselling]] services and offers. Some merchants provide [[mobile web]] sites that are customized for the smaller screen and limited user interface of a mobile device.

===In-application mobile phone payments===

Payments can be made directly inside an application running on a popular smartphone operating system, such as Google Android. Analyst firm Gartner expects in-application purchases to drive 41 percent of app store (also referred to as mobile software distribution platforms) revenue in 2016.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.zdnet.com/article/in-app-payments-more-profitable-than-paid-apps/ |title=In-app payments more profitable than paid apps |work=ZDNet |access-date=2013-01-25}}</ref> In-app purchases can be used to buy [[virtual goods]], new and other mobile content and is ultimately billed by mobile carriers rather than the app stores themselves.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://paidcontent.org/2011/10/11/419-ericsson-enables-in-app-android-payments-via-carrier-bills |title=Ericsson Enables In-App Android Payments Via Carrier Bills |work=PaidContent |access-date=2013-01-25|date=11 October 2011 }}</ref> Ericsson's IPX mobile commerce system is used by 120 mobile carriers to offer payment options such as try-before-you-buy, rentals and subscriptions.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.fiercemobilecontent.com/story/ericsson-brings-carrier-billing-app-payments/2011-10-12 |title=Ericsson brings carrier billing to in-app payments |work=Fierce Mobile Content |url-status=usurped |access-date=2013-01-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111211040551/http://www.fiercemobilecontent.com/story/ericsson-brings-carrier-billing-app-payments/2011-10-12 |archive-date=11 December 2011 }}</ref>

=== Mobile marketing and advertising ===
{{Main|Mobile marketing}}
In the context of mobile commerce, '''mobile marketing''' refers to marketing sent to mobile devices. Companies have reported that they see better responses from mobile marketing campaigns than from traditional campaigns. The primary reason for this is the instant nature of customer decision-making that mobile apps and websites enable. The consumer can receive a marketing message or discount coupon and, within a few seconds, make a decision to buy and go on to complete the sale - without disrupting their current real-world activity.

For example, a busy mom tending to her household chores with a baby in her arm could receive a marketing message on her mobile about baby products from a local store. She can, within a few clicks, place an order for her supplies without having to plan ahead for it. There is no need to reach for her purse to find credit cards, no need to log into her laptop to recall the store's web address, and no need to find a babysitter while she runs to the store.

Research demonstrates that consumers of mobile and wireline markets represent two distinct groups who are driven by different values and behaviors, and who exhibit dissimilar psychographic and demographic profiles.<ref>Schejter, A., Serenko, A., Turel, O., and Zahaf, M. (2010) "[http://www.aserenko.com/papers/policy_implications_serenko_proof.pdf Policy implications of market segmentation as a determinant of fixed-mobile service substitution: What it means for carriers and policy makers]", Telematics and Informatics, 27(1), 90-102.</ref> What aspects truly distinguish between a traditional online shopper from home and a mobile on-the-go shopper? Research shows that how individuals relate to four situational dimensions- place, time, social context and control determine to what extent they are ubiquitous or situated as consumers.<ref>Banerjee, Syagnik (Sy) and Dholakia, Ruby Roy, "Situated or Ubiquitous? A Segmentation of Mobile E-Shoppers" (4 January 2013). International Journal of Mobile Communications, Forthcoming. Available at SSRN: http://ssrn.com/abstract=2196689</ref> These factors are important in triggering m-commerce from e-commerce. As a result, successful mobile commerce requires the development of marketing campaigns targeted to these particular dimensions and according to user segments.

==Influence on youth markets{{Anchor|Mobile Commerce's Influence on Youth Markets}}==

Mobile media is a rapidly changing field. New technologies, such as [[WiMax]], act to accelerate innovation in mobile commerce. Early pioneers in mobile advertising include [[Vodafone]], [[Orange (telecommunications)|Orange]], and [[SK Telecom]]. An empirical study shows that over 70% of mobile commerce users are under the age of 25, as of 2019.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jimenez |first1=Nadia |last2=San-Martin |first2=Sonia |last3=Puente |first3=Nuria |title=The path to mobile shopping compatibility |journal=The Journal of High Technology Management Research |date=May 2019 |volume=30 |issue=1 |pages=15–26 |doi=10.1016/j.hitech.2018.12.006|s2cid=158795631 |hdl=10259/9772 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

Mobile devices are heavily used in South Korea to conduct mobile commerce. Mobile companies in South Korea believed that mobile technology would become synonymous with the youth lifestyle, based on their experience with previous generations of South Koreans. "Profitability for device vendors and carriers hinges on high-end mobile devices and the accompanying killer applications," said Daniel Longfield.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.frost.com/prod/servlet/press-release.pag?docid=72554850 |title=Mobile Device Vendors Turn to Growth Opportunities in Emerging Markets to Combat Fall in Average Price per Unit |last=Castilla |first=Mireya |date=16 June 2006 |website=Frost & Sullivan |access-date=29 December 2017}}</ref>

== Payment methods ==
{{Main|Mobile payment}}
Consumers can use multiple forms of payment in mobile commerce, including:
* [[Contactless payment]] for in-person transactions through a mobile phone (such as [[Apple Pay]] or [[Google Pay (payment method)|Google Pay]]).  In a system like [[EMV]], these are interoperable with contactless credit and debit cards.
* [[Premium-rate telephone number]]s, which apply charges to the consumer's long-distance bill
* Mobile-Operator Billing allows charges to be added to the consumer's mobile telephone bill, including deductions to pre-paid calling plans
* [[Credit card]]s and [[debit card]]s 
** Some providers allow credit cards to be stored in a phone's [[SIM card]] or secure element
** Some providers are starting to use [[host card emulation]], or HCE (e.g. [[Google Wallet]] and [[Softcard]])
** Some providers store [[credit card]] or [[debit card]] information in the cloud; usually in [[Tokenization (data security)|tokenized]].  With tokenization, payment verification, authentication, and authorization are still required, but payment card numbers don't need to be stored, entered, or transmitted from the mobile device
* [[Micropayment]] services
* [[Stored-value card]]s, often used with mobile-device application stores or music stores (e.g. iTunes)

== App design ==
[[Interaction design]] and [[User interface design|UX design]] has been at the core of the m-commerce experience from its conception, producing apps and mobile web pages that create highly usable interactions for users.<ref>Preece, J., Rogers, Y. and Sharpe, H. (2011), ''Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction'', Fourth., John Wiley & Sons, USA.</ref> However, much debate has occurred as to the focus that should be given to the apps. In recent research, Parker and Wang<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Parker|first1=Christopher J.|last2=Wang|first2=Huchen|title=Examining hedonic and utilitarian motivations for m-commerce fashion retail app engagement|journal=Journal of Fashion Marketing and Management|date=12 September 2016|volume=20|issue=4|pages=487–506|doi=10.1108/JFMM-02-2016-0015|url=https://www.research.manchester.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/examining-hedonic-and-utilitarian-motivations-for-mcommerce-fashion-retail-app-engagement(98defb8e-c227-43b1-824b-9f8b55b61cca).html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190529122337/https://www.research.manchester.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/examining-hedonic-and-utilitarian-motivations-for-mcommerce-fashion-retail-app-engagement(98defb8e-c227-43b1-824b-9f8b55b61cca).html|url-status=dead|archive-date=29 May 2019}}</ref> demonstrated that within [[fashion]] m-Commerce apps, the degree that the app helps the user shop (increasing convenience) was the most prominent function. Such use examples might be through design cues that help the user find their products with minimal search.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Parker|first1=Christopher J.|last2=Henninger|first2=Claudia E.|title=Enabling Sustainable Behaviours Through M-Commerce App Design: Focus on The Fast Fashion Industry|date=2018|publisher=Greenleaf Publishing|location=Sheffield|isbn=9781351058346|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-31aDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT89|access-date=17 May 2018}}</ref> 
Additionally, shopping for others was a motivator for engaging in m-commerce apps with a great preference for close integration with [[social media]]. Research shows that culture makes a significant difference in people's motivation to engage in shopping, where Western consumers - for example - have significantly different motivations to Chinese consumers.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Parker |first1=Christopher J. |last2=Wenyu |first2=Lu |title=What influences Chinese fashion retail? Shopping motivations, demographics and spending |journal=Journal of Fashion Marketing and Management|date=13 May 2019 |volume=23 |issue=2 |pages=158–175 |doi=10.1108/JFMM-09-2017-0093|s2cid=170031856 |url=https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/2134/36823 }}</ref>

== App commerce ==

The popularity of apps has given rise to the latest iteration of mobile commerce: app commerce. This refers to retail transactions that take place on a native mobile app. App commerce is said to perform better than both desktop and mobile web when it comes to browsing duration and interactions.<ref name="MicrosoftBizBlog">[https://blogs.business.microsoft.com/en-gb/2017/08/01/rising-challenge-mobile-retail/ Microsoft UK Small and Medium Business Blog | Rising to the challenge of mobile in retail]</ref> Average order value is reportedly greater with retail apps than traditional ecommerce, and conversion rates on apps are twice that of mobile websites.<ref name="MicrosoftBizBlog" /> The convenience and tailored user experience of apps make them a preferred [[shopping channel]] for mobile-savvy consumers.

== Mobile Device Shopping Trends ==

Shopping search behavior also differs between mobile and non-mobile devices. An analysis of Google Shopping search data found that the mobile share of shopping searches was higher on weekends and holidays, particularly for products associated with more impulsive purchases or greater privacy needs.<ref>{{cite SSRN
 |last1=Qian

 |last2=Du

}}</ref> Mobile applications serve as a means to ensure positive user experience, seamless interaction, and increased revenues for e-commerce. According to a [[DesignRush]] report,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://finance.yahoo.com/news/mobile-device-shopping-grown-21-091500900.html|website=finance.yahoo.com|title=Mobile Device Shopping Has Grown 21%: How Apps Are Cashing in on Holiday Shopping & Which Agencies Can Help|language=en-US|access-date=2018-12-19}}</ref> mobile applications are expected to generate $189 billion by 2020. Moreover, a study by Forrester shows that mobile devices will be leveraged to facilitate over $1 trillion in sales in 2018.
